html:
The seat of government of the Republic of Venice and the home of its doge, on the waterfront beside St Mark's Basilica. Under one roof it held the doge's rooms, the councils, the law courts and a prison. The first palace was begun after 810, when Doge Agnello Participazio moved the government here from Malamocco; it burned in a revolt against Doge Pietro IV Candiano in 976 and was rebuilt under Doge Sebastiano Ziani in the 1170s.

The Gothic palace seen today was begun about 1340, when the Great Council had grown too large for the old palace. The wing on the lagoon came first. From 1424 Doge Francesco Foscari had it carried along the Piazzetta, ending in the Porta della Carta, the ceremonial gate by Giovanni and Bartolomeo Bon (1438 to 1442). Its open arcade and loggia below a solid upper wall became the model for Venetian Gothic palaces such as the Ca' d'Oro.

Fires in 1483, 1574 and 1577 destroyed rooms and paintings by Bellini, Carpaccio and Titian. The Great Council chamber, 53 m by 25 m, was rebuilt in the old style rather than to new designs by Palladio, and repainted by Veronese and Tintoretto, whose Paradise fills the wall behind the doge's throne. A frieze shows the doges, with a black cloth in place of Marino Faliero, who tried to seize power in 1355. Soon after 1600 the Bridge of Sighs was built to link the palace to new prisons across the canal. After the republic fell in 1797 the palace held offices; it has been a museum since 1923.
